justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, which I placed around 346–347. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the current price with only a small expected move, reflecting the assumption that short-term momentum and recent trading patterns would persist without a major catalyst. For the one-week estimate, I nudged the price slightly higher to 349, incorporating a mild positive drift consistent with whatever broader trend appeared to be in place. The one-month estimate of 352 extends that drift further, essentially extrapolating a gradual, low-conviction upward bias while acknowledging that mean-reverting forces and changing conditions make any directional call increasingly uncertain over longer horizons.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical volatility at each time horizon, scaled by the square root of time in the conventional way. The one-day interval of roughly plus or minus 8 points is fairly tight, reflecting that most assets don't move dramatically in a single session absent a shock. The one-week interval widens to plus or minus 16 points, and the one-month interval expands to plus or minus 32 points, all of which are consistent with an annualized volatility assumption in the moderate range. I also factored in some additional uncertainty beyond pure statistical volatility because macroeconomic conditions, central bank communications, and geopolitical developments can produce non-normal, fat-tailed moves that simple historical vol would underestimate.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include surprise central bank decisions or unexpected inflation data releases, which can generate large, rapid repricing across asset classes. On the downside, a broader risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, a credit event, or a sudden deterioration in economic data could push the price well below my lower bounds. On the upside, an unexpectedly dovish policy pivot or a strong positive economic surprise could drive prices above my upper bounds. Liquidity conditions also matter — thin markets can amplify moves beyond what fundamentals alone would justify, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where compounding shocks become more likely.

Finally, I want to be transparent that my estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. I don't have real-time data access, so my baseline price level and recent trend assessment could themselves be miscalibrated if the market had already moved significantly before this forecast was constructed. That structural limitation means my intervals should probably be treated as somewhat wider in practice than the numbers I stated, and users should update them against any fresh information they have about recent price action.
